patient.chief_complaint: Worsening bilateral leg numbness and foot pain for 4 years
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Thompson is a 68-year-old White male with a 16-year history of type 2 diabetes and significant cardiovascular comorbidities who presents to the neurology clinic with a 4-year history of progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness and foot pain. He describes the initial symptom as a gradual onset of numbness in both feet, beginning in the toes and progressively spreading proximally to the mid-shin. Over the past year and a half, he has developed superimposed burning pain, particularly severe at night, making it difficult to sleep. He describes the sensation as walking on hot coals sometimes, and other times his feet feel completely numb and wooden. He reports that he has had two foot ulcers in the past year that took several weeks to heal, and his vascular surgeon has been monitoring him for peripheral arterial disease as well. He has noted difficulty sensing temperature in the shower and frequently checks his feet in the mirror because he cannot feel them reliably. He has also noticed some weakness when trying to scrunch his toes and difficulty rising onto his toes. He denies hand numbness, weakness in the arms, double vision, or swallowing difficulties. His blood sugars have been erratic with his most recent HbA1c described as very high by his endocrinologist. He has not had a formal neurological evaluation previously for these symptoms. He denies alcohol abuse, toxic chemical exposure, or new medications other than his current regimen.

specialized_test.impression: Severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Sural and superficial peroneal SNAPs are absent bilaterally; peroneal motor amplitudes are severely reduced; tibial motor amplitude reduced with prolonged F-wave. Mild ulnar sensory reduction in the upper extremity may reflect early proximal extension. EMG shows active (fibrillation potentials 2+, positive sharp waves 2+) and chronic denervation in distal lower extremity muscles; extensor digitorum brevis shows no recordable activity. No demyelinating features — no temporal dispersion, no conduction block. Findings are consistent with a severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.result: Orthostatic hypotension: BP drop 28/12 mmHg at 2 minutes

output.impression: Moderate-to-severe autonomic dysfunction — QSART absent at distal leg and foot; mildly reduced at forearm (0.7 uL/cm2). Cardiovagal studies markedly abnormal (E:I ratio 1.02; Valsalva ratio 1.10, both below normal thresholds). Significant orthostatic hypotension on tilt table testing (BP drop 28/12 mmHg at 2 minutes). Findings are consistent with moderate-to-severe predominantly distal autonomic neuropathy with cardiovagal involvement. Clinical correlation recommended.

Near-complete loss of intraepidermal nerve fibers distally (IENFD 0.3 fibers/mm; reference >7.0) with moderate reduction proximally (proximal thigh 4.2 fibers/mm; reference >9.0). Findings confirm severe small fiber neuropathy with a length-dependent gradient. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Sural nerve biopsy shows severe axonal neuropathy — markedly reduced myelinated fiber density (3,200/mm2; reference >6,000/mm2), predominantly large myelinated fiber loss with also reduced small unmyelinated fibers. Microangiopathic changes present: capillary basement membrane thickening, increased endoneurial collagen, mildly thickened vessel walls. No epineurial vasculitis. Congo red staining negative for amyloid. Findings are consistent with severe axonal neuropathy with microangiopathic vessel changes. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Intensive glycemic control reduces neuropathy 60% in T1DM; legacy effect sustained
Improved glycemic control reduces microvascular complications including neuropathy in T2DM
HbA1c target <7% reduces neuropathy risk; foot exam annually or more frequently if high risk

output.summary: Large randomized controlled trials (DCCT/EDIC, UKPDS) provide strong evidence that intensive glycemic control (HbA1c target <7%) reduces the incidence and slows progression of diabetic peripheral neuropathy. Published ADA standards recommend annual foot examination and more frequent assessment in high-risk patients. FDA-approved symptomatic pharmacotherapy for painful diabetic neuropathy includes duloxetine and pregabalin. Metformin use is associated with impaired B12 absorption in epidemiological studies, with functional deficiency confirmed by elevated methylmalonic acid.
